newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfricans seek pardon for race murder of US student. [CORRECTED 17:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: SAfricans seek pardon for race murder of US student. [CORRECTED 17:00 GMT]

text.p: Four black youths who murdered white American student Amy Biehl in a township attack four years ago are appealing for amnesty for the crime, South Africa's "truth commission" said on Friday. (Corrects number of youths from three to four.)
The four, sentenced to 18 years in jail for the murder, have applied for amnesty and their hearing will take place next month, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission said in a statement.

Biehl, a 26-year-old Fulbright scholar, was stoned, stabbed and battered to death by a mob as she drove friends home in Cape Town's Guguletu township in August 1993. She had been due to return to her California home the next day.
Her family, from Newport Beach, Orange County, will attend the hearing on July 8.
The judges who presided at the killers' trials found that Biehl was killed simply because she was white.
The murderers said they were supporters of the black radical Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), which has told the commission that its members targeted whites in the fight against apartheid.
Three PAC members have also asked for amnesty for the St James Church massacre in July 1993.

In that attack, 11 people were killed and over 20 seriously wounded when gunmen burst into a suburban Cape Town church in July 1993, opening fire with automatic weapons and hurling grenades packed with nails.

Three PAC members jailed for the Heidelberg Tavern massacre in Cape Town on December 30, 1994, are also asking the truth commission for pardon. Four people were killed and five wounded when gunmen shot wildly at revellers in the crowded pub.
Their hearing will also take place in July.

The truth commission, mandated to grant amnesty to those who make full confessions, was set up in 1995 to uncover as much as possible about political crimes and human rights abuses during the apartheid era.
